newsitem.title: USA: Governors decline to slam U.S. clean air plan.
newsitem.headline: Governors decline to slam U.S. clean air plan.

text.p: Divided over economic and health priorities, state governors on Sunday backed down from a budding confrontation with the Clinton administration over a controversial proposal to tighten U.S. air quality standards.

The governors' action followed a move by the Environmental Protection Agency on Saturday to ask a court to approve a 60-day delay of the new clean air rules, which would allow time for the public to comment on the plan.
The EPA set a Feb. 18 deadline for comments on its November proposal to set stricter limits on soot and smog-forming ozone because the agency was under a court order to issue new rules this June.

States, counties and cities asked the EPA in December to give them an extra two months to review the proposal, which would put more than 200 counties out of compliance with air standards and force them to impose new pollution controls.

Instead of urging the EPA to prove there was strong scientific evidence of the need for tougher standards, as proposed by Ohio Republican Governor George Voinovich, the governors' compromise resolution said the rules must strike a balance between health protection and "the burdens of unnecessary regulation."

"I thought it was premature for us to say the (proposed) standards were bad," said New Jersey Gov. Christine Whitman, a Republican, who led the effort to tone down the clean air policy statement by the National Governors' Association at its annual winter meeting.
Whitman told reporters she believed new clean air standards should be based on protecting public health, and not just on calculations of the economic costs and health benefits of tighter limits.

"The nation's governors will work with EPA, the Congress and others in evaluating the proposed rulemaking to ensure the protection of public health in the most cost-effective and efficient manner possible," said the resolution, passed by the NGA natural resources committee and set to be approved on Tuesday by the full NGA.
Whitman said the governors had not yet reached any consensus on the clean air proposal and did not want to issue a strong statement, which would have influenced Congress.
"If we had said we didn't like the standards, that would have had an impact in the Congress," she told reporters after the committee meeting.
Congress is set to begin hearings on EPA's proposal soon.
The next full review of the governors' clean air policy will be in July. "It's going to be tough to come up with a (new) policy," Whitman said.

The natural resources committee passed a range of other environmental resolutions, including a new policy urging the federal government to come up with drought assistance for states, similar to other disaster aid plans.
